official_title: Do the people of the state of Missouri approve the act of the General Assembly entitled "House Bill No. 1 (2025 Second Extraordinary Session)," which repeals Missouri's existing congressional plan, and replaces it with new congressional boundaries that keep more counties intact? State and local governmental entities estimate no costs or savings.
plain_summary: In September 2025 the legislature redrew Missouri's eight U.S. House districts in the middle of the decade, mainly splitting the Kansas City area so Republicans would likely win seven of eight seats instead of six. A citizen referendum petition (People Not Politicians Missouri) gathered enough signatures to put that law on hold, and on September 3, 2026 the Missouri Supreme Court unanimously ordered it onto this ballot. Proposition A asks whether the new map should become law. Either way, the November 2026 U.S. House races use the old 2022 map; the court said the 2025 plan 'is not the law and has never been the law.' If approved, the new map takes effect 30 days later and would first apply in 2028.
yes_means: The 2025 map (House Bill 1) becomes law and is used for U.S. House elections starting in 2028.
no_means: The 2025 map is rejected. Missouri keeps the congressional map drawn in 2022.
current_law: The 2022 map is in effect: six Republican-leaning districts and two Democratic-leaning ones (MO-1 in St. Louis and MO-5 in Kansas City). Under the 2022 map, Webster Groves and Clayton are in MO-1 and Ballwin is in MO-2. The 2025 map has been suspended since December 2025, when the referendum petition qualified; the Supreme Court confirmed on Sept 3, 2026 that it cannot be used 'unless and until' voters approve it. (A separate 4-3 ruling on March 24, 2026 found the 2025 map itself did not violate the state constitution.)
fiscal_impact: Official fair ballot language: 'If passed, this measure will have no impact on taxes.' State and local governmental entities estimate no costs or savings.
confusing_wording_note: This is a referendum, so the usual 'yes = change' instinct still holds but the framing is backwards from the petition. The petition was to STOP the map; the ballot asks whether to APPROVE it. YES = the legislature's new map. NO = keep the old map. If you signed the petition, the matching vote is NO. Two more traps: the ballot title says the new map 'keep[s] more counties intact,' which is the sponsors' framing (a court made the Secretary of State strip other argumentative language in March 2026). And nothing on this ballot changes the November 2026 House races, which use the 2022 map no matter what.

supporters_case.text: Supporters (Gov. Mike Kehoe, the Missouri Republican Party, Republican legislative leaders, President Trump) call it the 'Missouri First Map' and say a 7-1 map 'better represents Missouri's values in Congress' and 'better protects counties and rural communities.' Act for Missouri, a conservative volunteer guide, calls it 'a close call' and leans yes.

opponents_case.text: Opponents (People Not Politicians Missouri, the Missouri Democratic Party, Missouri AFL-CIO, Sierra Club, and some Republicans) say redrawing districts mid-decade with no new census 'allows DC political consultants to rig Missouri elections,' that the map 'would split Kansas City into three districts,' and that 'a NO vote will allow Missouri voters to pick their politicians.'

official_title: Shall the Missouri Constitution be amended to: Repeal the 2024 voter-approved Amendment providing reproductive healthcare rights, including abortion through fetal viability; Allow abortions for rape and incest (under twelve-weeks' gestation), emergencies, and fetal anomalies; Allow legislation regulating abortion; Ensure parental consent for minors' abortions; Prohibit gender transition procedures for minors? State governmental entities estimate no costs or savings. Greene County estimates it may experience an unknown increase in tax revenue. Other local governmental entities estimate no costs or savings.
plain_summary: Repeals the abortion-rights amendment Missouri voters passed in November 2024 (that year's Amendment 3, now Article I, Section 36) and replaces it with language that lets the legislature ban most abortions. Abortion would stay legal in medical emergencies, for fetal anomalies, and for rape or incest only up to 12 weeks. It requires parental or judicial consent for minors, limits public funding, and lets the legislature regulate providers and clinics. It also writes into the constitution a ban on gender-transition surgery, cross-sex hormones and puberty blockers for minors (already state law through August 2027).
yes_means: Repeal the 2024 right to reproductive freedom; limit abortion to emergencies, fetal anomalies, and rape or incest before 12 weeks; and put the ban on gender-transition care for minors in the constitution.
no_means: Keep the 2024 amendment: the constitutional right to abortion until fetal viability stays as it is, and the minors' transition-care ban stays a statute, not a constitutional rule.
current_law: Since the 2024 amendment took effect (Dec 5, 2024), the Missouri Constitution protects 'reproductive freedom' and abortion is legal until fetal viability; clinics in St. Louis, Kansas City and Columbia resumed abortions in 2025 after court rulings. Gender-transition treatments for minors are banned by a 2023 state law (SB 49) whose main provisions expire in August 2027.
fiscal_impact: Official fair ballot language: 'If passed, this measure will not increase or decrease taxes.' State entities estimate no costs or savings; Greene County estimates a possible unknown increase in tax revenue.
confusing_wording_note: Two different 'Amendment 3's. The 2024 Amendment 3 LEGALIZED abortion. This 2026 Amendment 3 REPEALS it. 'Yes on 3' signs this year are the anti-abortion side; 'repeal and replace Amendment 3' stickers mean the same thing. A YES vote bans most abortions; a NO vote keeps abortion legal. The legislature's original summary never used the word 'repeal'; a Cole County judge ordered it rewritten in September 2025 after an ACLU lawsuit, which is why the ballot now opens with 'Repeal the 2024 voter-approved Amendment.' Read the exceptions carefully: 'emergencies' is not a general health exception, and the rape and incest exception ends at 12 weeks. The gender-transition clause is a separate subject bundled into the same yes/no.

supporters_case.text: Supporters (Missouri Right to Life, the Missouri Republican Party, Gov. Mike Kehoe, the Missouri Catholic Conference, the Her Health, Her Future PAC) call it 'a measure to protect women and children' and 'a way to craft policy more protective of mom and baby,' and say it still protects women in emergencies and victims of rape and incest.

opponents_case.text: Opponents (the Stop the Ban campaign: Planned Parenthood, ACLU of Missouri, Abortion Action Missouri; plus the League of Women Voters of Missouri, the Missouri Democratic Party, SEIU, Sierra Club) call it a 'trojan horse to reinstate Missouri's total abortion ban,' say voters already decided this in 2024, and say the minors' transition clause is bundled in to win votes it couldn't win on abortion alone.

official_title: Shall the Missouri Constitution be amended to: expand the initiative and referendum petition process by making it a fundamental right; allow courts to revise ballot summaries through lawsuits; prohibit the legislature from weakening initiative or referendum powers; prohibit the legislature from changing or repealing laws enacted through the initiative process, or passing laws similar to those rejected by referendum, without approval from at least 80% of both chambers; and preserve existing majority vote and signature requirements for initiative and referendum petitions? State and local governmental entities estimate no costs or savings.
plain_summary: Makes it much harder for the legislature to undo laws that voters passed by petition. Right now lawmakers can change or repeal a voter-approved statute by simple majority (they did that in 2025 with the paid-sick-leave law from 2024's Prop A). Under Amendment 6, changing a voter-passed law would need 80% of both the House and Senate, and even then the change goes back to voters. It also bars the legislature from making petitions harder, lets courts rewrite unfair ballot summaries, keeps today's signature and simple-majority rules, and applies back to initiatives passed since January 1, 2010. Sponsored by the citizen group Respect Missouri Voters; the Secretary of State tried to keep it off the ballot and the Supreme Court overruled him on Sept 3, 2026.
yes_means: Voter-passed laws can only be changed with 80% of both legislative chambers plus a public vote; the legislature can't weaken the petition process; courts can fix biased ballot summaries.
no_means: No change. The legislature keeps its current power to amend or repeal voter-approved statutes by simple majority.
current_law: Citizens can propose statutes and constitutional amendments by petition and force referendums on new laws. A voter-approved statute (not a constitutional amendment) can be changed by the legislature like any other law. Signature requirements are 5% of voters in two-thirds of congressional districts for a statute and 8% for an amendment; passage is a simple statewide majority. In August 2026 voters rejected Amendment 4, which would have required amendments to also win a majority in every congressional district.
fiscal_impact: Official fair ballot language: 'If passed, this measure will not increase or decrease taxes.' State and local governmental entities estimate no costs or savings.
confusing_wording_note: Five provisions in one yes/no. The one that matters most is the 80% rule. Note the official 'no' statement says current law 'already give[s] citizens the right to propose initiatives and referenda,' which is true; the fight is over what happens AFTER voters pass something. It is the mirror image of August's Amendment 4 (which would have made passing initiatives harder, and failed 80-20): Amendment 6 makes repealing them harder. 'Fundamental right' in the first clause has no settled legal meaning here. The look-back to 2010 means already-passed measures (Medicaid expansion, minimum wage, marijuana, 2024's abortion amendment and sick leave) would get the new protection.

supporters_case.text: Supporters (Respect Missouri Voters, the Missouri Democratic Party, Missouri AFL-CIO, Sierra Club) say 'the ballot initiative process really is a check and balance against politicians' and that lawmakers should not be able to repeal what voters just approved, as they did with paid sick leave.

opponents_case.text: Opponents (the Missouri Chamber of Commerce, the Missouri Republican Party, Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, Attorney General Catherine Hanaway, Liberty Alliance) say it would 'permanently handcuff lawmakers' from fixing bad or misleading measures, that 'billionaire-funded ballot campaigns could leave lawmakers unable to change voter-approved policies,' and that it 'will create significant risk for Missouri businesses.'

official_title: Shall the Missouri Constitution be amended to establish a permanent public endowment fund to support state government instead of taxing Missouri residents, prohibit the General Assembly from appropriating or diverting the fund, and eliminate state-imposed taxes once the fund generates sufficient revenue to replace them? State and local governmental entities estimate no costs or savings.
plain_summary: Creates a state investment account called the Show-Me Prosperity Fund, invested in S&P 500 index funds, with the long-term goal of growing large enough that its earnings could replace state taxes. The amendment puts no money in the fund; the legislature would decide how to seed it (the sponsor, Rep. Colin Wellenkamp, R-St. Charles, modeled a one-time $250 million deposit). Lawmakers couldn't spend from it until the Treasurer certifies the earnings can cover state taxes, withdrawals are capped at 3% a year, and once taxes are eliminated the legislature couldn't bring them back unless the fund fails. The sponsor's own estimate is that reaching the goal would take about 100 years.
yes_means: Create the Show-Me Prosperity Fund in the constitution, with its spending lockbox and the eventual-tax-elimination rules.
no_means: No fund is created. Nothing changes.
current_law: Missouri has no sovereign-wealth-style endowment. State operations are funded year to year by income, sales and other taxes through the regular budget.
fiscal_impact: Official fair ballot language: 'If passed, this measure will have no immediate impact on taxes but could lead to the elimination of state-imposed taxes if the net investment earnings of the fund become sufficient to support that outcome.' State and local entities estimate no costs or savings, because the amendment itself deposits nothing.
confusing_wording_note: The title says the fund would 'support state government instead of taxing Missouri residents,' which sounds like a tax cut. It is not. No tax changes on passage, no money goes in on passage, and the sponsor says the payoff is roughly a century away. Voting yes creates an empty, locked box and a set of rules for a future legislature to fill it. The real questions are where the seed money would come from (unspecified) and what happens in a recession if the state ever depends on it.

supporters_case.text: Supporters (sponsor Rep. Colin Wellenkamp, the Missouri Republican Party) call it 'a long term pay-it-forward' that could grow to 'several trillion dollars' and promote it 'as a path toward eliminating taxes.'

opponents_case.text: Opponents (Missouri Budget Project, the Missouri Democratic Party, Missouri AFL-CIO, Act for Missouri on the right) say it 'leaves too many unanswered questions,' names no funding source, could pull money from schools and services, and would underperform in a downturn when the state most needs revenue. The Tax Foundation raised similar recession concerns without taking a position.

official_title: Shall the Missouri Constitution be amended to support law enforcement by preserving the right of citizens to elect a county sheriff, prohibiting the removal of a county sheriff except by a writ of quo warranto, and recognizing the office of sheriff as part of the administration of justice? State and local governmental entities estimate no costs or savings.
plain_summary: Moves the elected office of county sheriff from state law into the state constitution, so the legislature couldn't abolish it or change its listed duties without a public vote. It also narrows how a sheriff can be removed: only through a 'quo warranto' court action started by the state Attorney General, which cuts out local prosecutors. The official 'yes' statement itself notes counties already elect sheriffs every four years under current statute. ST. LOUIS COUNTY VOTERS: it does not apply to you. The amendment exempts St. Louis City, St. Louis County and St. Charles County, which have their own charter arrangements (St. Louis County has a police department, not an elected sheriff running law enforcement).
yes_means: Elected sheriffs and their duties go into the constitution, and only the Attorney General can start a removal case.
no_means: No change. Sheriffs stay elected under state statute, and current removal procedures (including local prosecutors) remain.
current_law: Missouri statute requires each county to elect a sheriff to a four-year term and sets the duties. Removal can be pursued through quo warranto by the Attorney General or the local prosecuting attorney, and through other statutory processes. St. Louis County's charter puts county policing under an appointed police chief; its elected sheriff handles court security and process service.
fiscal_impact: Official fair ballot language: 'If passed, this measure will not increase or decrease taxes.' State and local entities estimate no costs or savings.
confusing_wording_note: The title opens with 'support law enforcement' and 'preserving the right of citizens to elect a county sheriff,' but nobody is proposing to take that right away; it already exists in statute. The practical change is the removal rule: today a local prosecutor or the AG can bring a quo warranto case; under Amendment 8 only the AG can. 'Quo warranto' is a lawsuit asking a court to remove someone from office. The 'constitutional sheriff' movement, which holds that sheriffs may refuse to enforce laws they consider unconstitutional, is the backdrop; the sponsor says the measure adds 'no more power.' Also: it exempts the three St. Louis-area jurisdictions by name, so a St. Louis County vote on it is about the rest of the state.

supporters_case.text: Supporters (sponsor Sen. Jill Carter, R-Granby; Rep. Bennie Cook; Osage County Sheriff Michael Bonham; the Missouri Republican Party) say it protects the office from legislators angry at sheriffs: 'This just moves it into the constitution to ensure that our sheriffs can never, never be taken away from us,' and 'We're not giving them any more power.'

opponents_case.text: Opponents (the Missouri Democratic Party; Rep. Aaron Crossley) say it would make it 'extremely difficult for voters to remove a bad sheriff' by handing removal to the AG alone, and object to locking undefined terms like 'traitors' into the constitution. Some conservatives (Rep. Bryant Wolfin, Act for Missouri) oppose it from the other side as not going far enough and for the exclusions.
